en: So now that we know what a reverse proxy is,
the question of course is what exactly is
this compose.yaml file about? I mean, I
mentioned before that we have this
Dockerfile which configures the environment
for our web app. And in there we simply have
a bunch of instructions that install
required software and make sure that in the
end we have the web app ready to use.
But what's this other file about and where's
the Dockerfile for Traefik?
Well, Traefik doesn't have a Dockerfile in
our project. And to understand this,
it's important to understand that Docker
containers are actually built based on
so-called Docker images.
Now, this Dockerfile I showed you for the
web app does technically define such an
image. It defines an image for our
container.
This image then is turned into the actual
container by the instructions in the
compose.yaml file. For our web app here,
we have this build part in this
configuration and here we point at our
Dockerfile and this simply does create this
Docker image and then instruct Docker
overall to create a container based on that
image. That is how you can think about that.
So the Dockerfile defines the image, the
Docker Compose file then makes sure that
this image gets used for this app container.
That is the idea here.
And we will therefore be
launching
our web app based on this Compose file later
on the VPS.
In that Compose file, we then have
additional instructions as well. For
example, how this container should be
restarted. So for example, that it should be
restarted whenever it crashes unless we
stopped it explicitly.
We can add so-called volumes, which is a
more advanced concept, but the idea here
simply is that
data written in the container actually
survives container restarts by being
mirrored to the hard drive of the host that
runs the container.
So the host is our VPS, keep in mind, and
volumes simply are a link from data in the
container onto our host.
The network here simply defines that the
other container I'll get back to, which
contains the reverse proxy, is in the same
network as our app container so that the 2
can talk to each other.
And then these labels here are used by the
reverse proxy container for registering our
app as an app that is managed by our reverse
proxy. So these labels are really just there
for the reverse proxy, the traffic proxy, to
detect and use our web app correctly. And
then we got some logging set up here which
makes sure that log messages written by the
web app that's running in our container are
written to the host. Just as we wanna keep
the app data, the database data that's
written in the container and wanna persist
that on the host, we also wanna persist our
logs. So we write them to our localhost in
the end and we also restricted the max size
of the log files to 10 megabytes and the max
number of log files that are written to 5 so
that we don't flood our hard drive.
But that's the idea behind the Compose file
and the idea behind images. So why does
Traefik not have a Dockerfile then? Well,
because here we have an image
entry, an image property in the
configuration, which we didn't have for our
web app. There we had build instead. And the
idea simply is that we build the image for
the web app based on our own Dockerfile,
whereas we use a prebuilt image here for
Traefik. And that is simply the official
image by the Traefik team, so to say. So we
don't need a Dockerfile. Dockerfile here
because they already created one for us.
And indeed they publish that on GitHub. So
there you could actually find Dockerfiles
and you find a link to one example
Dockerfile attached. So we could
also
try to build our own Dockerfile and copy
this one, for example, but they already did
that for us, did publish it to
the Docker Hub, which is a Docker registry
for images. So we can just pull it in like
this. That's the only reason why we don't
have a Dockerfile.
Again, if you wanna dive deeper into Docker,
I have a dedicated course on that, but this
should explain what we generally have here.
